en: The pillar of the Muslims,
Surely they will destroy it,” I thought.
“Will they dig my pit?
If the Chinese press hard,
They will bring my misfortune to the boil.”
My heart was terribly troubled,
Tears poured from my eyes.
Unable to bear my distress,
I camped along broad Talas.
Your father would not lie with me;
I was a neglected wife for six months.
Brave but without sense,
Your foolish father thought:
“Ak-kula, this year,
I shall fatten properly,” he thought.
Letting Ak-kula loose,
While your father lay without a care,
I had the face of the earth searched;
Without letting one person know,
Without letting a single soul notice,
I had Ak-kula brought in.
I had sand spread beneath him,
Fed him barnyard millet from the rice fields,
Had him exercised to a sweat each day;
Feeding him barley from a hanging feedbag,
I had him exercised to a sweat each month.
“When he joins the spear-fight,
A spear's point will pierce him,
He will meet an untimely death,” I thought.
I made its lining of silk,
For six months I worked its patterns with my teeth.
Its collar gold, its sleeves brass,
Double mail, with lark-eye rings,
A kele cloth coat, a roomy vest,
The handsome Ak-olpok,
That would keep him from defeat in battle,
That no arrow's point could reach,
That thrusting steel could not penetrate,
I twisted its weft eightfold.
Saying, “I grieved, a neglected wife,”
Your mother, without resentment,
Made it stout for battle.
For your father, generous Manas,
I fashioned his coat to fit,
And tended his horse on fresh pasture.
The lame smith Bölökbay,
With his forty guards at their head—
I gathered forty smiths.
Should the forty Chinese tribes, the emperor's people,
Suddenly come swarming,
So he could stand unflinching,
I had bullets cast of steel.
I did not look to get them for nothing.
When slung, the mirror of his shoulder blades,
When going into battle, Ak kelte—
The comfort of his life held in trust—
I made Ak kelte ready then.
I readied his weapons,
While I, the fierce woman, stood there.
Of your foster-father, brave Chubak,
Let me begin to tell:
His father, Akbaltay,
Was a khan famed throughout the world.
Upon Akbaltay's head
There rested sacred power.
Those who saw his imposing presence trembled.
Akbaltay studied five years in Mecca.
He received a letter from the caliph,
Received a blessing from a prince,
And was called a renowned mighty hero.
They had come to live in Altay.
Your grandfather, that swine of a khan, and Akbaltay
Were driven out as offenders,
And went to broad Altay.
A star moved in the sky;
Your grandfather and Akbaltay
Became friends for the world to come,
Their sheep shared neighboring folds,
They shared their food as comrades,
Shared the dust when scouting,
Shared their lives in battle.
Once Akbaltay, who honored ancestral spirits,
When Chubak fled to him, said:
“Freed from Altay, I, your father,
Settled along broad Kashkar.
Akbaltay amassed countless livestock;
When his herds filled all around,
I took sixty wives.
Not one of the sixty bore a child;
I was left without an heir.
All four kinds of livestock,
For a single child to follow me,
I spent and scattered.
The shrines shaped like a saddle's waist
I walked around time after time.
I traveled everywhere,
With sixty wrestlers at my side,
When the people moved uphill,
At the season horses' tongues turn black,
In the desert of Mediyan,
On the bank of Kayyp-Bulak,
You were the child I found.
When I slaughtered ninety beasts for your feast,
When I gave you the name Chubak,
Until you reached twelve years,
I cherished and raised you.
Seen today, gone tomorrow—
My dear son, listen to my words!
When you reached the age of twelve,
Finding no mountain to hurl yourself against,
Finding no foe to fight,
You went and settled in Talas.
You became a warrior-companion of Jakyp's
Only son, Manas.
To wage war together on your foes,
To press your claims together,
You spoke invoking God;
You swore an oath unto death.
You chewed grains of white wheat together,
Together you held the holy Koran.
You set out, making the earth split;
Seventy times you pledged friendship.
Since you went to Manas,
You reached the Afghans.
Untouched by your hand—
How could Jerkent remain unharmed?
You brought seven holy teachers from Mecca,
And established them in seven places.
I am not taking back my words:
You made every place you reached crawl.
Who had not seen your face pale with rage—
Not one among the people remained.
Where you had not chased a giant—
Not one place remained.
Who had not heard your shrill battle cry—
Not one among the people remained.
You raided the Afghans, took gold coins,
Took a thousand dark-eyed ones,
Ravaged Ombu and took booty.
You and your scourge, Manas,
Broke through their midst and made a road!
To Manas, blessed by Kyzyr,
You were a friend until Judgment Day.
Manas is your companion.
Quarreling with your companion,
Why did you part from him, my son?
Take heed, my Chubak:
Together with that lion Manas,
It is your time to be a sultan.
Offended by gossip,
What has happened, my dear son?
If you join with your generous lord,
But for your own brutish folly,
It is time for you two to conquer!
Beyond the ridge you have the Chinese;
You have many foes to crush.
My colt Chubak, blessed by Kyzyr,
Your father Akbaltay speaks—heed me!
Can one who listens to gossip prosper?
Can one who believes idle words
Be a Muslim in faith?
One of seven days brings death.
My son, I have words for you:
On the coming Day of Judgment,
For Khan Manas himself,
My son, you may become a black donkey.
Offended by words spoken behind your back,
My son, you have come fleeing here!
Offended by words spoken behind his back,
My son, can a fugitive count as a man?
Offended by your blood-shedding lord,
Can one prosper, slinking here in fear?
Your horse grew fat; you grew strong.
Coming from many places, forty companions,
You became the forty who shook the world.
You grew to manhood and became a warrior,
An equal of brave men's sons.
You became a house built in Talas,
Became a khan over many lands.
No reckless raider struck your village.
While that Manas was there,
No one remained who could withstand you.
Your fathers' graves, you forty companions!
There is no cause for sorrow if you die!
Rising in rebellion, making ready,
At the head of the forty, Kyrgylchal,
The mad old man swollen with pride at forty—
Offended by one corrupt dog,
Kyrgylchal, head of the forty,
The old man chief of forty companions,
The old man whose thoughts are wicked,
Who has thought up much wickedness—
Your fleet steed, Manas the panther,
He never ceased saying, ‘He ruined him.’
When the fool spread gossip,
Chubak, you took offense and lost your senses.
Against your old friend Manas,
You prepared to act as an enemy.
Now, my son Chubak, heed my words;
You will settle in a wondrous place.
If you stubbornly refuse to heed me,
Chubak, you will be all the more an unbeliever.
If you obey, my son, you are a hero;
My son, if you disobey, you are an unbeliever!”
When Khan Baltay, in wrath,
Upon your fierce warrior Chubak
Pronounced a curse instead of blessing,
That his father would disown him—
When your lion Chubak saw this,
Taking a red-tailed elephant,
Your precious Chubak obeyed.
The tent with six guy ropes
He had folded this way and that,
To the steed bred in Alay
Had it brought and loaded.
All the ammunition,
Then your fierce Chubak
Had loaded onto the swift camel.
From the skilled spearmen
He took a band of nine;
From the mighty wielders of battle-axes
He took another band of nine.
Every piece of equipment
He had loaded on the red elephant.
The Sarts of broad Kashkar
He had play a great komuz, its back an armful,
And their dutar;
His sixty or so Sarts
He had all sing songs.
The capable men mounted;
He set them all moving.
Chubak mounted and set out,
Traveling by night, not by day.
His father Akbaltay,
Saying “Amen,” spread his palms:
“My only colt, Chubak,
May your guiding omen be excellent.
If you die, my colt,
May your faith be your companion!
You were Chubak the lion;
I was Akbaltay, your father.
May the Forty Chiltens, your Kyzyr Iliyas,
Cry out and turn their gaze upon you.
The dark, fierce panther,
Your renowned, fierce Manas—
May he remain your companion!”
Akbaltay turned about,
And stood saying, “Amen.”
Akbaltay's Chubak,
Receiving his father's blessing,
Mounted and left Alay.
Skirting broad Kashkar,
Grieving the host he had gathered,
Halting by day, traveling by night,
Crossing passes, treading stone,
Your Chubak journeyed without stopping,
